name: Chapter 2: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
description: Principal value branches, graphs, standard values, properties and identities, simplification by substitution, composite functions, equations, and exam-style problems.

cards.term: When does a function f have an inverse?
cards.definition: Exactly when f is one-one and onto (bijective). Then f⁻¹ has domain = range of f and range = domain of f

cards.term: Why do the six trig functions have no inverse on their natural domains?
cards.definition: They are periodic, so not one-one (sin 0 = sin π). So we restrict each to a piece where it is a bijection

cards.term: Principal branch of sin⁻¹ comes from restricting sin to [−π/2, π/2]
cards.definition: sin is not one-one on R; restricting to [−π/2, π/2] makes it a bijection onto [−1,1]; that piece defines the principal branch of sin⁻¹

cards.term: What is a “branch” of an inverse trig function? What is the principal value branch?
cards.definition: Each restriction interval (e.g. [−π/2, π/2], [π/2, 3π/2], …) gives a different branch. The branch with the range containing 0 / the smallest positive angles is the principal value branch. Unless told otherwise we always use it

cards.term: Domains and ranges of inverse trig functions
cards.definition: sin⁻¹: domain [−1, 1] → range [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹: domain [−1, 1] → range [0, π]; tan⁻¹: domain R → range (−π/2, π/2); cot⁻¹: domain R → range (0, π); sec⁻¹: domain R − (−1, 1) → range [0, π] − {π/2}; cosec⁻¹: domain R − (−1, 1) → range [−π/2, π/2] − {0}

Give the domain and the range (principal value branch) of each function.

sin⁻¹domain [−1, 1] → range [−π/2, π/2]
cos⁻¹domain [−1, 1] → range [0, π]

Domain of f⁻¹ = range of f; range of f⁻¹ = restricted domain of f

cards.term: Principal value ranges: right half circle vs upper half circle
cards.definition: sin^-1, tan^-1, cosec^-1 take values in the right half (-pi/2 to pi/2, negative allowed); cos^-1, cot^-1, sec^-1 in the upper half (0 to pi)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Principal values on the circle

Which half of the unit circle holds the principal values of sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹? Which half holds cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹?

Think: which angles have negative sine? Negative cosine?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Principal values on the circle

Which half of the unit circle holds the principal values of sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹? Which half holds cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹?

Right half (quadrants IV and I, angles from −π/2 to π/2): sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹. They can be negative.

Upper half (quadrants I and II, angles from 0 to π): cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹. Never negative.

Excluded end-points: tan⁻¹ (±π/2), cot⁻¹ (0, π), cosec⁻¹ (0), sec⁻¹ (π/2).

cards.term: Mnemonic: which inverse functions can give negative values?
cards.definition: sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹ (range in [−π/2, π/2]). cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹ are never negative (range in [0, π]). The “co-” functions cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹ share (0, π); sec⁻¹ follows cos⁻¹

cards.term: What is a “principal value”?
cards.definition: The value of an inverse trig function that lies in its principal branch. Example: the principal value of sin⁻¹(½) is π/6, not 5π/6 or π/6 + 2π

cards.term: Trap: is sin⁻¹x the same as (sin x)⁻¹?
cards.definition: No. sin⁻¹x = arcsin x is the inverse function. (sin x)⁻¹ = 1/sin x = cosec x. sin⁻¹(½) = π/6 but (sin ½)⁻¹ ≈ 2.09

cards.term: If y = sin⁻¹x, what can you say about sin y and about y?
cards.definition: sin y = x with −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2 (and x ∈ [−1, 1]). Always check the range of y: that is what makes the answer unique

cards.term:
Ex 2.1 Q13: If sin⁻¹x = y, then
(A) 0 ≤ y ≤ π
(B) −π/2 ≤ y ≤ π/2
(C) 0 < y < π
(D) −π/2 < y < π/2
cards.definition: The range of sin⁻¹ is the closed interval: (B)

cards.term: Which inverse trig functions have gaps in the range, and where?
cards.definition: sec⁻¹ never equals π/2 (sec y = ∞ there) cosec⁻¹ never equals 0 tan⁻¹ never reaches ±π/2 cot⁻¹ never reaches 0 or π

cards.term: sin⁻¹ graph is the mirror image of sin on [−π/2, π/2]
cards.definition: sin⁻¹ : [-1,1] -> [-pi/2, pi/2] is the reflection of sin restricted to [-pi/2, pi/2] in y = x; increasing and odd

cards.term: How is the graph of f⁻¹ obtained from the graph of f?
cards.definition: Reflect in the line y = x: (a, b) on f ↔ (b, a) on f⁻¹. That also swaps domain and range

cards.term: cos⁻¹ graph
cards.definition: y = cos⁻¹x; domain [−1, 1]; range [0, π]. Decreasing; cos⁻¹0 = π/2; cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x, so the graph is symmetric about (0, π/2).

cards.term: tan⁻¹ graph
cards.definition: y = tan⁻¹x; domain R; range (−π/2, π/2). Increasing, odd, with horizontal asymptotes y = ±π/2 (never reached).

cards.term: cot⁻¹ graph
cards.definition: y = cot⁻¹x; domain R; range (0, π). Decreasing, with horizontal asymptotes y = 0 and y = π; cot⁻¹x = π/2 − tan⁻¹x.

cards.term: sec⁻¹ graph
cards.definition: y = sec⁻¹x; domain R − (−1, 1); range [0, π] − {π/2}. Two branches; asymptote y = π/2; sec⁻¹x = cos⁻¹(1/x).

cards.term: cosec⁻¹ graph
cards.definition: y = cosec⁻¹x; domain R − (−1, 1); range [−π/2, π/2] − {0}. Two branches; asymptote y = 0; cosec⁻¹x = sin⁻¹(1/x); odd function.

cards.term: Which inverse trig graphs are increasing? Decreasing?
cards.definition: Increasing: sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, and sec⁻¹ on each of its two branches. Decreasing: cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, and cosec⁻¹ on each of its two branches. Sanity check: cos⁻¹ and cot⁻¹ fall from π to 0

cards.term: Which inverse trig functions are odd, which are not?
cards.definition: Odd: sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹. Neither even nor odd: cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹, which satisfy f(−x) = π − f(x) (symmetric about the point (0, π/2))

cards.term: Which inverse trig functions have horizontal asymptotes?
cards.definition: tan⁻¹: y = ±π/2. cot⁻¹: y = 0 and y = π. sec⁻¹: y = π/2. cosec⁻¹: y = 0. sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ have none (bounded domain)

cards.term: Complementary inverse trig identities from a right triangle
cards.definition: sin^-1 x + cos^-1 x = pi/2 (x in [-1,1]); tan^-1 x + cot^-1 x = pi/2; sec^-1 x + cosec^-1 x = pi/2 (|x|>=1); triangle with hypotenuse 1 and leg x

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x

In this right triangle (hypotenuse 1, one leg x), name the two acute angles. What is their sum?

Complementary acute angles.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x

In this right triangle (hypotenuse 1, one leg x), name the two acute angles. What is their sum?

The angle opposite the side x has sine x: it is sin⁻¹x. The other angle has cosine x: it is cos⁻¹x. Acute angles of a right triangle add to π/2:

sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2, for x ∈ [−1, 1]. Same idea: tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2 (x ∈ R) and sec⁻¹x + cosec⁻¹x = π/2 (|x| ≥ 1).

The same triangle also gives sin⁻¹x = tan⁻¹(x/√(1 − x²)) = cos⁻¹√(1 − x²) for 0 ≤ x < 1.

cards.term: Negative arguments: sin⁻¹(−x), tan⁻¹(−x), cosec⁻¹(−x)?
cards.definition: sin⁻¹(−x) = −sin⁻¹x, tan⁻¹(−x) = −tan⁻¹x, cosec⁻¹(−x) = −cosec⁻¹x (odd functions)

cards.term: Negative arguments: cos⁻¹(−x), cot⁻¹(−x), sec⁻¹(−x)?
cards.definition: cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x, cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹x, sec⁻¹(−x) = π − sec⁻¹x. Check: cos⁻¹(−½) = π − π/3 = 2π/3

cards.term: Reciprocal arguments: sin⁻¹(1/x), cos⁻¹(1/x), tan⁻¹(1/x)?
cards.definition: sin⁻¹(1/x) = cosec⁻¹x, cos⁻¹(1/x) = sec⁻¹x (both for |x| ≥ 1); tan⁻¹(1/x) = cot⁻¹x for x > 0 (for x < 0: cot⁻¹x − π)

cards.term: Example 1: principal value of sin⁻¹(1/√2)?
cards.definition: sin y = 1/√2 with y ∈ [−π/2, π/2]: π/4

cards.term: Example 2: principal value of cot⁻¹(−1/√3)?
cards.definition: cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹x = π − π/3 = 2π/3 (range (0, π), cot 2π/3 = −1/√3 ✓)
Negative, in [−π/2, 0]: −π/6
cos π/6 = √3/2 and π/6 ∈ [0, π]: π/6

cards.term: Ex 2.1 Q3: cosec⁻¹(2)?
cards.definition: sin y = ½: π/6 (y ∈ [−π/2, π/2], y ≠ 0)
tan⁻¹ is odd: −tan⁻¹√3 = −π/3
π − π/3 = 2π/3
−π/4
cos y = √3/2 → π/6
tan y = 1/√3, y ∈ (0, π): π/6
π − π/4 = 3π/4

cards.term: Ex 2.1 Q10: cosec⁻¹(−√2)?
cards.definition: −cosec⁻¹√2 = −π/4
π/4 + 2π/3 − π/6 = (3π + 8π − 2π)/12 = 3π/4
π/3 + 2(π/6) = 2π/3
π/3 − (π − π/3) = π/3 − 2π/3 = (B) −π/3

cards.term: When is sin(sin⁻¹x) = x? When is sin⁻¹(sin x) = x?
cards.definition: sin(sin⁻¹x) = x for x ∈ [−1, 1] (always safe). sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only for x ∈ [−π/2, π/2]. Same pattern for the others with their own principal intervals

cards.term: Which composite is always safe: f(f⁻¹(x)) or f⁻¹(f(x))?
cards.definition: f(f⁻¹(x)) = x whenever x is in the domain of f⁻¹. f⁻¹(f(x)) = x only if x lies in the principal interval

cards.term: Example 6: sin⁻¹(sin 3π/5)?
cards.definition: 3π/5 ∉ [−π/2, π/2]. Use sin(3π/5) = sin(π − 3π/5) = sin(2π/5), and 2π/5 ∈ [−π/2, π/2]: 2π/5

cards.term: Compute sin⁻¹(sin 10). (Radians)
Compute cos⁻¹(cos 10), tan⁻¹(tan 5).
cards.definition: cos⁻¹(cos 10) = 4π − 10 ≈ 2.566 (in [0, π]). tan⁻¹(tan 5) = 5 − 2π ≈ −1.283 (in (−π/2, π/2))

cards.term: Compute cos⁻¹(cos 7π/6) and tan⁻¹(tan 7π/6). (Misc Q1, Q2 style)
cards.definition: cos⁻¹(cos 7π/6) = cos⁻¹(cos 5π/6) = 5π/6. tan⁻¹(tan 7π/6) = tan⁻¹(tan π/6) = π/6 (tan has period π)

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q10: sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3)?
cards.definition: sin(2π/3) = sin(π/3) = √3/2 → π/3

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q11: tan⁻¹(tan 3π/4)?
cards.definition: tan(3π/4) = −1 → −π/4
7π/6 ∉ [0, π]; cos(7π/6) = cos(2π − 7π/6) = cos(5π/6): (B) 5π/6
sin⁻¹(−½) = −π/6, so sin(π/3 + π/6) = sin(π/2) = (D) 1
π/3 − (π − π/6) = π/3 − 5π/6 = (B) −π/2

cards.term: Find sin(cos⁻¹(3/5)) and tan(sin⁻¹(5/13)).
cards.definition: Triangle 3-4-5: sin = 4/5. Triangle 5-12-13: tan = 5/12. (Draw the right triangle with the angle and read the ratio.)

cards.term: Method: evaluate trig(inverse trig(x)) such as sec²(tan⁻¹2) + cosec²(cot⁻¹3).
cards.definition: Use identities directly: sec²θ = 1 + tan²θ = 1 + 4 = 5; cosec²φ = 1 + cot²φ = 1 + 9 = 10. Total 15

cards.term: Simplify cos(2 tan⁻¹(1/7)) and sin(2 tan⁻¹(1/3)).
cards.definition: With t = tan θ: cos 2θ = (1 − t²)/(1 + t²) = (48/49)/(50/49) = 24/25; sin 2θ = 2t/(1 + t²) = (2/3)/(10/9) = 3/5

cards.term: Double-angle forms of tan⁻¹: 2 tan⁻¹x = ?
cards.definition: sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) for |x| ≤ 1 cos⁻¹((1 − x²)/(1 + x²)) for x ≥ 0 tan⁻¹(2x/(1 − x²)) for |x| < 1

cards.term: Example 3(i): prove sin⁻¹(2x√(1 − x²)) = 2 sin⁻¹x. For which x is it valid?
cards.definition: x = sin θ: sin⁻¹(2 sin θ cos θ) = sin⁻¹(sin 2θ) = 2θ, valid only if 2θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2], that is −1/√2 ≤ x ≤ 1/√2. Outside this range the result changes (see the next card)

cards.term: Example 3(ii): sin⁻¹(2x√(1 − x²)) = 2 cos⁻¹x for which x?
cards.definition: x = cos θ: sin⁻¹(sin 2θ) = 2θ needs 2θ ∈ [0, π/2] (x ≥ 0), so it holds for 1/√2 ≤ x ≤ 1. Consistency: there sin⁻¹(2x√(1 − x²)) = π − 2 sin⁻¹x = 2 cos⁻¹x

cards.term: Triple-angle forms: 3 sin⁻¹x = ? 3 cos⁻¹x = ? 3 tan⁻¹x = ?
cards.definition: 3 sin⁻¹x = sin⁻¹(3x − 4x³) for x ∈ [−½, ½] 3 cos⁻¹x = cos⁻¹(4x³ − 3x) for x ∈ [½, 1] 3 tan⁻¹x = tan⁻¹((3x − x³)/(1 − 3x²)) for |x| < 1/√3

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q1: prove 3 sin⁻¹x = sin⁻¹(3x − 4x³), x ∈ [−½, ½].
cards.definition: x = sin θ, θ ∈ [−π/6, π/6]. sin⁻¹(3 sin θ − 4 sin³θ) = sin⁻¹(sin 3θ) = 3θ, since 3θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2]. = 3 sin⁻¹x

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q2: prove 3 cos⁻¹x = cos⁻¹(4x³ − 3x), x ∈ [½, 1].
cards.definition: x = cos θ, θ ∈ [0, π/3]. cos⁻¹(4cos³θ − 3cos θ) = cos⁻¹(cos 3θ) = 3θ since 3θ ∈ [0, π]. = 3 cos⁻¹x

cards.term: Sum formula for tan⁻¹: tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = ?
cards.definition: tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) if xy < 1; π + tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) if xy > 1 and x, y > 0; −π + … if xy > 1 and x, y < 0

cards.term: tan⁻¹ addition formula and the xy > 1 correction
cards.definition: tan^-1 x + tan^-1 y = tan^-1((x+y)/(1-xy)) if xy<1; add pi if xy>1 and x,y>0 (subtract pi if x,y<0); tan^-1 2 + tan^-1 3 = 3pi/4

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y

tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3 = ? The formula gives tan⁻¹((2 + 3)/(1 − 6)) = tan⁻¹(−1). Is the answer −π/4?

Add the angles geometrically first.
advancedHtml.backHtml:
tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y

tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3 = ? The formula gives tan⁻¹((2 + 3)/(1 − 6)) = tan⁻¹(−1). Is the answer −π/4?

Both angles are in (0, π/2) so their sum is in (0, π): it cannot be negative. 63.4° + 71.6° = 135° = 3π/4.

tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y = tan⁻¹((x + y)/(1 − xy)) only when xy < 1. If xy > 1 (x, y > 0) add π: tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3 = π + tan⁻¹(−1) = 3π/4. (If xy > 1 with x, y < 0, subtract π.)

cards.term: Difference formula for tan⁻¹: tan⁻¹x − tan⁻¹y = ?
cards.definition: tan⁻¹((x − y)/(1 + xy)), valid for xy > −1

cards.term: sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹y = ? and cos⁻¹x + cos⁻¹y = ? (standard forms)
cards.definition: sin⁻¹(x√(1 − y²) + y√(1 − x²)) when the sum lies in [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹(xy − √(1 − x²)√(1 − y²)) when x + y ≥ 0

cards.term: Prove tan⁻¹(1/2) + tan⁻¹(1/3) = π/4.
Prove tan⁻¹1 + tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3 = π.
cards.definition: tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3 = 3π/4 (xy = 6 > 1, add π to tan⁻¹(−1)); plus π/4 = π

cards.term: Machin-type: 4 tan⁻¹(1/5) − tan⁻¹(1/239) = ?
cards.definition: π/4. 2 tan⁻¹(1/5) = tan⁻¹(5/12), 4 tan⁻¹(1/5) = tan⁻¹(120/119); subtract tan⁻¹(1/239) to get tan⁻¹1

cards.term: Telescoping: Σ tan⁻¹(1/(n² + n + 1)) for n = 1 to ∞?
cards.definition: tan⁻¹(1/(1 + n(n + 1))) = tan⁻¹(n + 1) − tan⁻¹n. Sum = lim tan⁻¹(N + 1) − tan⁻¹1 = π/2 − π/4 = π/4

cards.term: Trap: is sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹y always sin⁻¹(x√(1−y²) + y√(1−x²))?
cards.definition: No. For x = y = 1: sin⁻¹1 + sin⁻¹1 = π, but the right side is sin⁻¹(0) = 0. The formula needs the sum to stay in [−π/2, π/2]

cards.term: Substitutions for simplifying inverse trig expressions
cards.definition: √(1 − x²): x = sin θ (or cos θ); √(1 + x²): x = tan θ; √(x² − 1): x = sec θ; √(a² − x²): x = a sin θ; √(a² + x²): x = a tan θ; √((1 − x)/(1 + x)), √(1 + x) ± √(1 − x): x = cos 2θ; (2x)/(1 + x²), (1 − x²)/(1 + x²): x = tan θ (gives sin 2θ, cos 2θ); 3x − 4x³, 4x³ − 3x: x = sin θ / cos θ (gives sin 3θ, cos 3θ)

advancedHtml.frontHtml:
Substitutions

Which substitution simplifies each expression?

√(1 − x²)?
√(1 + x²)?
√(x² − 1)?
√(a² − x²)?
√(a² + x²)?
√((1 − x)/(1 + x)), √(1 + x) ± √(1 − x)?
(2x)/(1 + x²), (1 − x²)/(1 + x²)?
3x − 4x³, 4x³ − 3x?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Substitutions

Which substitution simplifies each expression?

√(1 − x²)x = sin θ (or cos θ)
√(1 + x²)x = tan θ
√(x² − 1)x = sec θ
√(a² − x²)x = a sin θ
√(a² + x²)x = a tan θ
√((1 − x)/(1 + x)), √(1 + x) ± √(1 − x)x = cos 2θ
(2x)/(1 + x²), (1 − x²)/(1 + x²)x = tan θ (gives sin 2θ, cos 2θ)
3x − 4x³, 4x³ − 3xx = sin θ / cos θ (gives sin 3θ, cos 3θ)

After substituting, use an identity to get one trig function of a multiple angle, then cancel with the inverse. Always check the interval

cards.term: Example 4: write tan⁻¹(cos x/(1 − sin x)), −3π/2 < x < π/2, in simplest form.
cards.definition: cos x/(1 − sin x) = (cos²(x/2) − sin²(x/2))/(cos(x/2) − sin(x/2))² = (cos(x/2) + sin(x/2))/(cos(x/2) − sin(x/2)) = tan(π/4 + x/2). Since π/4 + x/2 ∈ (−π/2, π/2): π/4 + x/2

cards.term: Example 5: write cot⁻¹(1/√(x² − 1)), x > 1, in simplest form.
cards.definition: x = sec θ: √(x² − 1) = tan θ so cot⁻¹(cot θ) = θ = sec⁻¹x

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q3: simplify tan⁻¹((√(1 + x²) − 1)/x), x ≠ 0.
cards.definition: x = tan θ: (sec θ − 1)/tan θ = (1 − cos θ)/sin θ = tan(θ/2). So ½ tan⁻¹x

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q4: simplify tan⁻¹√((1 − cos x)/(1 + cos x)), 0 < x < π.
cards.definition: (1 − cos x)/(1 + cos x) = tan²(x/2): tan⁻¹(tan(x/2)) = x/2 (x/2 ∈ (0, π/2))

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q5: simplify tan⁻¹((cos x − sin x)/(cos x + sin x)), −π/4 < x < 3π/4.
cards.definition: Divide by cos x: (1 − tan x)/(1 + tan x) = tan(π/4 − x), and π/4 − x ∈ (−π/2, π/2): π/4 − x

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q6: simplify tan⁻¹(x/√(a² − x²)), |x| < a.
cards.definition: x = a sin θ: tan⁻¹(sin θ/cos θ) = θ = sin⁻¹(x/a)

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q7: simplify tan⁻¹((3a²x − x³)/(a³ − 3ax²)), a > 0, −a/√3 < x < a/√3.
cards.definition: x = a tan θ: (3 tan θ − tan³θ)/(1 − 3 tan²θ) = tan 3θ, and 3θ ∈ (−π/2, π/2): 3 tan⁻¹(x/a)

cards.term: Ex 2.2 Q8: tan⁻¹[2 cos(2 sin⁻¹(1/2))]?
cards.definition: 2 sin⁻¹(½) = π/3, 2 cos(π/3) = 1, tan⁻¹1 = π/4
sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) = 2 tan⁻¹x and cos⁻¹((1 − y²)/(1 + y²)) = 2 tan⁻¹y. So tan(tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y) = (x + y)/(1 − xy)

cards.term: Simplify tan⁻¹(√(1 + x²) − x).
cards.definition: x = tan θ, θ ∈ (−π/2, π/2): sec θ − tan θ = (1 − sin θ)/cos θ = tan(π/4 − θ/2), and π/4 − θ/2 ∈ (0, π/2). So π/4 − ½ tan⁻¹x

cards.term: Simplify sin⁻¹(2x/(1 + x²)) for x ≥ 1 (a common trap).
cards.definition: x = tan θ with θ ∈ [π/4, π/2): sin⁻¹(sin 2θ) and 2θ ∈ [π/2, π), so = π − 2θ = π − 2 tan⁻¹x. (Not 2 tan⁻¹x, which holds only for |x| ≤ 1.)

cards.term: Simplify cos⁻¹((1 − x²)/(1 + x²)) for x ≥ 0 and for x < 0.
cards.definition: x ≥ 0: 2 tan⁻¹x. x < 0: the value must be ≥ 0, so −2 tan⁻¹x (= 2 tan⁻¹|x|)

cards.term: Misc Q1: cos⁻¹(cos 13π/6)?
cards.definition: 13π/6 = 2π + π/6, so cos(13π/6) = cos(π/6): π/6

cards.term: Misc Q2: tan⁻¹(tan 7π/6)?
cards.definition: tan(7π/6) = tan(π/6): π/6

cards.term: Misc Q3: prove 2 sin⁻¹(3/5) = tan⁻¹(24/7).
Misc Q4: prove sin⁻¹(8/17) + sin⁻¹(3/5) = tan⁻¹(77/36).
Misc Q5: prove cos⁻¹(4/5) + cos⁻¹(12/13) = cos⁻¹(33/65).
Misc Q6: prove cos⁻¹(12/13) + sin⁻¹(3/5) = sin⁻¹(56/65).
Misc Q7: prove tan⁻¹(63/16) = sin⁻¹(5/13) + cos⁻¹(3/5).
Misc Q8: prove tan⁻¹√x = ½ cos⁻¹((1 − x)/(1 + x)), x ∈ [0, 1].
cards.definition: x = tan²θ: (1 − tan²θ)/(1 + tan²θ) = cos 2θ, and cos⁻¹(cos 2θ) = 2θ since 2θ ∈ [0, π/2]. So RHS = θ = tan⁻¹√x. ✓

cards.term: Misc Q9: prove cot⁻¹((√(1 + sin x) + √(1 − sin x))/(√(1 + sin x) − √(1 − sin x))) = x/2, x ∈ (0, π/4).
cards.definition: Write 1 ± sin x = (cos(x/2) ± sin(x/2))². The fraction becomes 2cos(x/2)/2sin(x/2) = cot(x/2), and x/2 ∈ (0, π/8). ✓
x = cos 2θ: √(1 + x) = √2 cos θ, √(1 − x) = √2 sin θ. Ratio (cos θ − sin θ)/(cos θ + sin θ) = tan(π/4 − θ). Answer π/4 − θ = π/4 − ½ cos⁻¹x

cards.term: Misc Q11: solve 2 tan⁻¹(cos x) = tan⁻¹(2 cosec x).
cards.definition: tan(2A) = 2cos x/(1 − cos²x) = 2 cos x/sin²x. Set equal to 2/sin x: cos x = sin x. x = nπ + π/4 (n ∈ Z)

cards.term: Misc Q12: solve tan⁻¹((1 − x)/(1 + x)) = ½ tan⁻¹x, x > 0.
cards.definition: LHS = π/4 − tan⁻¹x, so π/4 = (3/2) tan⁻¹x, tan⁻¹x = π/6: x = 1/√3

cards.term:
Misc Q13: sin(tan⁻¹x), |x| < 1, equals
(A) x/√(1 − x²)
(B) 1/√(1 − x²)
(C) 1/√(1 + x²)
(D) x/√(1 + x²)
cards.definition: Triangle with legs x and 1, hypotenuse √(1 + x²): sin = (D) x/√(1 + x²)

cards.term:
Misc Q14: sin⁻¹(1 − x) − 2 sin⁻¹x = π/2, then x =
(A) 0, ½
(B) 1, ½
(C) 0
(D) ½
cards.definition: Let θ = sin⁻¹x: sin⁻¹(1 − x) = π/2 + 2θ, so 1 − x = cos 2θ = 1 − 2x², giving x(2x − 1) = 0. x = ½ fails (sin⁻¹(½) − π/3 = −π/6 ≠ π/2), x = 0 works: (C) 0

cards.term: Domain of sin⁻¹(2x − 1)?
cards.definition: −1 ≤ 2x − 1 ≤ 1 → 0 ≤ x ≤ 1

cards.term: Domain of cos⁻¹(x² − 4)?
Domain of sec⁻¹(2x + 1)?
cards.definition: |2x + 1| ≥ 1 → 2x + 1 ≥ 1 or ≤ −1 → x ≥ 0 or x ≤ −1

cards.term: Range of f(x) = sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x + tan⁻¹x?
cards.definition: sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 on [−1, 1], so f = π/2 + tan⁻¹x with range [π/4, 3π/4]

cards.term: Range of f(x) = 2 sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x?
cards.definition: f = sin⁻¹x + π/2, x ∈ [−1, 1]: [0, π]

cards.term: Range of f(x) = cos⁻¹x − sin⁻¹x?
cards.definition: f = π/2 − 2 sin⁻¹x for x ∈ [−1, 1], and sin⁻¹x ∈ [−π/2, π/2]: [−π/2, 3π/2]

cards.term: Solve sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹(1 − x) = cos⁻¹x.
cards.definition: sin⁻¹(1 − x) = cos⁻¹x − sin⁻¹x = π/2 − 2 sin⁻¹x. Take sine: 1 − x = cos(2 sin⁻¹x) = 1 − 2x², so x(2x − 1) = 0. Both check: x = 0 gives π/2 = π/2; x = ½ gives π/6 + π/6 = π/3 = cos⁻¹½. x = 0 or ½

cards.term: Solve tan⁻¹(x − 1) + tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹(x + 1) = tan⁻¹3x.
cards.definition: tan⁻¹(x − 1) + tan⁻¹(x + 1) = tan⁻¹(2x/(2 − x²)). Adding tan⁻¹x and equating tan: x = 0 or x = ±1/2. All three satisfy the original

cards.term: Solve cos(2 sin⁻¹x) = 1/9.
cards.definition: cos 2θ = 1 − 2x² = 1/9 → x² = 4/9 → x = ±2/3

cards.term: Solve 2 tan⁻¹(sin x) = tan⁻¹(2 sec x).
cards.definition: tan(2A) = 2 sin x/(1 − sin²x) = 2 sin x/cos²x = 2/cos x → sin x = cos x: x = π/4 in (−π/2, π/2)

cards.term: Find the number of real solutions of tan⁻¹√(x(x + 1)) + sin⁻¹√(x² + x + 1) = π/2.
cards.definition: The second root needs x² + x + 1 ≤ 1, i.e. x² + x ≤ 0, while the first needs x² + x ≥ 0. So x² + x = 0: x = 0 or x = −1, and both give 0 + π/2 = π/2. Answer: 2 solutions

cards.term: If sin⁻¹x + sin⁻¹y + sin⁻¹z = 3π/2, find x + y + z.
cards.definition: Each term is at most π/2, so all three must equal π/2: x = y = z = 1. Hence x + y + z = 3

cards.term: If tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹y + tan⁻¹z = π then x + y + z = ?
cards.definition: tan(A + B + C) = 0 → x + y + z = xyz

cards.term:
MCQ: sin⁻¹(sin 5π/6) =
(a) 5π/6 (b) π/6 (c) −π/6 (d) 7π/6
cards.definition: sin(5π/6) = sin(π/6): (b) π/6
2π/3 + π/6 = (b) 5π/6

cards.term:
MCQ: tan⁻¹(1) + tan⁻¹(2) + tan⁻¹(3) =
(a) π (b) π/2 (c) 3π/4 (d) 0
cards.definition: (a) π
Complementary: (c) π/2

cards.term:
MCQ: the principal value of cosec⁻¹(−2) is
(a) π/6 (b) −π/6 (c) −π/3 (d) 5π/6
cards.definition: cosec⁻¹ is odd: (b) −π/6

cards.term:
MCQ: the domain of sin⁻¹(3x − 1) is
(a) [0, 2/3] (b) [−2/3, 0] (c) [0, 1] (d) R
cards.definition: −1 ≤ 3x − 1 ≤ 1 → 0 ≤ x ≤ 2/3: (a)
sum = π/2, cos = (b) 0

cards.term:
MCQ: sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x + tan⁻¹x for x > 0 =
(a) π (b) π/2 (c) 2π (d) 0
cards.definition: sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2 and tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2: (a) π

cards.term:
MCQ: sin⁻¹(x) + sin⁻¹(1 − x) = cos⁻¹x has a solution x =
(a) 1 (b) 0 (c) 1/2 (d) both (b) and (c)
cards.definition: x = 0: 0 + π/2 = π/2 ✓. x = ½: π/6 + π/6 = π/3 ✓. (d) (x = 1 fails: π/2 + 0 ≠ 0)

cards.term:
MCQ: the value of tan⁻¹2 + tan⁻¹3 is
(a) π/4 (b) 3π/4 (c) −π/4 (d) π/2
cards.definition: xy = 6 > 1, so add π to tan⁻¹(−1): (b) 3π/4

cards.term: Integer answer (JEE Main): the value of 12 (sin⁻¹(1/2) + tan⁻¹(1/√3) + cos⁻¹(1/2))/π is?
Integer answer: if tan⁻¹x + tan⁻¹(1/2) = π/4, then 3x =?

Assertion–Reason.
A: sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) = 2π/3.
R: sin⁻¹(sin x) = x for all x ∈ R.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A false, R false (d) A true, R false
cards.definition: (c): sin⁻¹(sin 2π/3) = π/3, and sin⁻¹(sin x) = x only for x ∈ [−π/2, π/2]

cards.term:
Assertion–Reason.
A: tan⁻¹x + cot⁻¹x = π/2 for all real x.
R: tan⁻¹x and cot⁻¹x are complementary angles for every x.
(a) Both true, R explains A (b) Both true, R does not (c) A true, R false (d) A false, R true
cards.definition: (a): for x > 0 the right-triangle picture; for x < 0 also true since tan⁻¹(−x) = −tan⁻¹x and cot⁻¹(−x) = π − cot⁻¹x

cards.term: True/False: cos⁻¹(−x) = −cos⁻¹x.
cards.definition: False. cos⁻¹(−x) = π − cos⁻¹x (cos⁻¹ takes only values in [0, π])

cards.term: True/False: tan⁻¹x has range [−π/2, π/2].
cards.definition: False. The range is the open interval (−π/2, π/2)

cards.term: 2-mark: find the principal value of sin⁻¹(−√3/2) + cos⁻¹(−√3/2).
cards.definition: sin⁻¹(−√3/2) = −π/3; cos⁻¹(−√3/2) = 5π/6. Sum π/2 (also directly from sin⁻¹t + cos⁻¹t = π/2)

cards.term: 3-mark: prove tan⁻¹(1/4) + tan⁻¹(2/9) = ½ cos⁻¹(3/5).
3-mark: prove sin⁻¹(3/5) − sin⁻¹(8/17) = cos⁻¹(84/85).
4-mark: find the value of x if tan⁻¹(2x) + tan⁻¹(3x) = π/4.
cards.definition: (5x)/(1 − 6x²) = 1 → 6x² + 5x − 1 = 0 → x = 1/6 or x = −1. x = −1 fails (both terms negative, sum ≠ π/4). x = 1/6

cards.term: 4-mark: prove that cos⁻¹(x) + cos⁻¹((x/2) + (√(3 − 3x²))/2) = π/3, x ∈ [½, 1].
cards.definition: x = cos θ, θ ∈ [0, π/3]: the second argument is (cos θ)/2 + (√3/2) sin θ = cos(θ − π/3), and π/3 − θ ∈ [0, π/3], so it gives π/3 − θ. Sum π/3 ✓

cards.term: Case-based: a 2 m tall screen has its lower edge 1 m above your eye level, at horizontal distance d. The viewing angle is tan⁻¹(3/d) − tan⁻¹(1/d). Find it for d = 3 m.
cards.definition: tan⁻¹(1) − tan⁻¹(1/3) = tan⁻¹((1 − 1/3)/(1 + 1/3)) = tan⁻¹(½) ≈ 26.6°. The angle is largest at d = √3 m, where the two tangents multiply to 1
